name: Erigeron breviscapus (breviscapine)
short: Mostly breviscapine injection added to usual care. Angina review, both groups: headache, dizziness, palpitations, nausea, itching, flushing, allergic reactions. Reviews: safety needs more study.
text: Most evidence comes from trials of breviscapine, which one review describes as a plant-derived flavonoid (none of the cited abstracts says that it comes from Erigeron breviscapus), mostly given as an injection added to conventional treatment; the cited abstracts give no human adverse-event data for the whole plant or for an extract taken by mouth. A meta-analysis of 36 trials (3058 patients) with unstable angina listed headache, dizziness, palpitations, nausea, abdominal distension, skin itching, flushes and allergic reactions as the main adverse reactions in the two groups, rated all studies as low quality, and said the injection's safety needs further study because of combined drugs and incomplete reporting. In acute cerebral infarction, a meta-analysis of 43 trials (4618 patients) found fewer adverse reactions with the injection plus conventional treatment than with conventional treatment alone and no serious adverse reactions, with low-certainty evidence; a meta-analysis of breviscapine injection in diabetic kidney disease could not judge its adverse reactions from the available evidence. A 2026 meta-analysis of 29 trials in coronary heart disease found no significant difference in adverse reactions (5 trials) and noted that data on acute cardiovascular events and deaths were insufficient or unreported. A review of the whole plant describes it as inhibiting platelet aggregation, and says acute and subacute toxicity studies showed it to be safe; none of the cited abstracts report bleeding. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
